lead: Metal cutting is the controlled removal of metal as chips to make a part with the required size and finish. This unit links the chip and force picture to tool geometry, tool life and the common machine tools. After it, you can compute cutting forces, tool life, machining time and MRR, and pick a lathe, drilling, milling or finishing operation.
about: This unit explains how a cutting tool turns a metal bar into chips and how machine tools use that action. Chapter 5.1 starts with chip formation, 5.2 resolves cutting forces, and 5.3 to 5.5 cover tool shape, material, wear and life. Chapters 5.6 to 5.8 apply these ideas to lathe, drilling, milling and gear cutting. Chapter 5.9 ends with abrasive finishing processes. After the unit, a student can read a tool signature, estimate forces, tool life, machining time and MRR, and choose a basic machine tool and finishing step.

chapters.idea: Cutting concentrates shear in a narrow zone and turns the uncut layer into a chip; orthogonal cutting is the two-dimensional case and oblique cutting is the three-dimensional case.
chapters.depth: Orthogonal cutting is two-dimensional: the cutting edge is perpendicular to the cutting velocity. Oblique cutting has the edge at inclination angle i; only a few universities teach it in detail, so cover effective rake and chip flow. Define cutting speed v (m/min), feed f (mm/rev), depth of cut d (mm), uncut chip thickness t₁, chip thickness t₂, rake angle α and shear angle φ. Cover chip formation stages, shear plane, chip thickness ratio r = t₁/t₂, tan φ = r cos α / (1 − r sin α), and chip types: continuous, discontinuous, continuous with built-up edge, and segmented. Introduce BUE and surface finish.

figure.title: Chip formation in orthogonal cutting
figure.aria: Block diagram of chip formation from tool engagement to chip leaving the shear plane.
figure.caption: The shear plane is where the uncut layer becomes a chip.

chapters.example: Orthogonal turning of a mild steel tube: uncut chip thickness t₁ = 0.25 mm, chip thickness t₂ = 0.60 mm, rake angle α = 10°. Find chip thickness ratio r and shear angle φ. Check: r = 0.417, φ ≈ 23.9°.
chapters.trap: Using r = t₂/t₁ instead of t₁/t₂; in oblique cutting the rake is the normal rake, not the side rake.
chapters.leave: Merchant forces to 5.2; tool angles to 5.3; machine tools to 5.6.

chapters.idea: The cutting force and thrust force resolve through the Merchant circle into friction on the rake face and shear on the shear plane.
chapters.depth: Resolve the cutting force Fc and thrust force Ft into friction and shear components on the rake face and shear plane. Define resultant R, friction angle β, friction coefficient μ = tan β, shear angle φ, shear force Fs, normal force Fn and shear area As = b t₁ / sin φ. Give F = Fc sin α + Ft cos α, N = Fc cos α − Ft sin α, and Merchant's relation 2φ + β − α = 90°. Show shear stress τ = Fs/As, cutting power P = Fc v, and specific cutting energy. Note that Merchant's relation is a minimum-energy approximation.

figure.title: Merchant force resolution
figure.aria: Block diagram resolving measured cutting forces into friction and shear forces.
figure.caption: The resultant force closes the Merchant circle and gives both friction and shear components.

chapters.example: Orthogonal cutting test: cutting force Fc = 1200 N, thrust force Ft = 600 N, rake angle α = 10°, uncut chip thickness t₁ = 0.25 mm, width of cut b = 2.5 mm, cutting speed v = 120 m/min. Find friction force F, normal force N, friction coefficient μ, friction angle β, shear angle φ by Merchant's relation, shear stress τ on the shear plane, and cutting power P. Check: F ≈ 799 N, N ≈ 1078 N, μ ≈ 0.742, β ≈ 36.6°, φ ≈ 31.7°, τ ≈ 592 MPa, P = 2.4 kW.
chapters.trap: Merchant's relation is a minimum-energy approximation; do not use it when friction or BUE is abnormal. Keep Fc and Ft in the same units and convert v to m/s for power in watts.
chapters.prereq: 5.1: chip thickness ratio and shear angle.
chapters.leave: Tool geometry to 5.3; tool life and wear to 5.5.

chapters.idea: A single-point tool is fully described by a fixed set of angles and a nose radius, written as the tool signature.
chapters.depth: Single-point tool parts: shank, face, flank, nose, cutting edge. Define back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, end cutting edge angle (ECEA), side cutting edge angle (SCEA), nose radius, and cutting edge inclination. Give the ASA seven-element tool signature in fixed order: back rake–side rake–end relief–side relief–ECEA–SCEA–nose radius. Some syllabi call it tool designation. Show sign conventions and how each angle affects chip flow, strength and finish. Mention orthogonal and oblique rake only as links to 5.1.

figure.title: ASA tool signature: 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5
figure.aria: Array of seven signature values with labels for each tool angle.
figure.caption: Each slot of the seven-element ASA signature sets one tool angle or the nose radius.

chapters.example: A single-point tool has ASA signature 0-10-6-6-8-15-0.5. Identify back rake, side rake, end relief, side relief, end cutting edge angle, side cutting edge angle, and nose radius. Check: back rake 0°, side rake 10°, end relief 6°, side relief 6°, ECEA 8°, SCEA 15°, nose radius 0.5 mm.
chapters.trap: The seven ASA values are always in fixed order; a number read in the wrong slot changes rake and relief.
chapters.leave: Tool material choice to 5.4; wear to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Tool material must keep hardness at cutting temperature, and cutting fluid controls heat, friction and chip removal.
chapters.depth: Tool materials: carbon tool steel, high-speed steel (18-4-1), cemented carbide (WC-Co), coated carbide (TiN, TiC, Al₂O₃), cermet, ceramic, cubic boron nitride (CBN) and diamond. Compare hot hardness, toughness, wear resistance and cost. Cutting fluids: functions cooling, lubrication, chip flushing, corrosion protection; types straight oil, soluble oil, semi-synthetic, synthetic; selection and application by flooding, mist and minimum quantity lubrication (only a few universities teach MQL). Link material choice to speed limits and to wear in 5.5.

figure.aria: Tree of cutting tool materials grouped by hot hardness and cost.
figure.caption: Materials are ordered roughly by hot hardness and cost, from carbon steel to diamond.

chapters.example: An 18-4-1 high-speed steel contains 18% W, 4% Cr, 1% V and 0.7% C by mass. For a 250 g tool blank, find the mass of tungsten, chromium, vanadium and carbon. Check: W = 45 g, Cr = 10 g, V = 2.5 g, C = 1.75 g.
chapters.trap: Carbide is not a single material; coated and uncoated grades differ. Water-mixed fluid is not universal for every metal.
chapters.leave: Wear mechanisms and Taylor life to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Tool wear grows with cutting temperature and time; Taylor's equation links cutting speed to tool life, and machinability ranks how easily a material cuts.
chapters.depth: Wear types: flank wear VB, crater wear, notch wear, chipping and built-up edge. Wear mechanisms: abrasion, adhesion, diffusion and oxidation. Tool life criteria: average flank wear 0.3 mm and maximum 0.6 mm are common ISO values. Taylor equation V Tⁿ = C; n ≈ 0.1 for HSS, 0.2–0.3 for carbide, 0.4–0.6 for ceramic. Machinability, machinability index, MRR = v f d for turning, and cutting speed, feed and depth of cut as operating parameters.

figure.aria: Plot of Taylor tool life falling sharply as cutting speed rises.
figure.caption: Tool life falls sharply as cutting speed rises on the Taylor curve.

chapters.example: Taylor tool life for a carbide tool is V T^0.25 = 300, with V in m/min and T in min. Find tool life at V = 120 m/min and at V = 240 m/min. Also find the speed for T = 60 min. Check: T ≈ 39.1 min, T ≈ 2.44 min, V ≈ 107.8 m/min.
chapters.trap: Taylor n is not negative; C has units that depend on n; tool life does not fall linearly with speed.
chapters.leave: CNC adaptive control to Unit 6; detailed machinability testing to advanced courses.

chapters.idea: A lathe rotates the workpiece and feeds a single-point tool to create cylindrical, faced and threaded surfaces.
chapters.depth: Lathe parts: bed, headstock, tailstock, carriage, cross-slide, compound rest, tool post, feed rod and lead screw. Types: speed lathe, bench lathe, engine lathe, toolroom lathe, capstan and turret lathe, automatic lathe; CNC lathe only as a cross-reference to Unit 6. Operations: turning, facing, chamfering, grooving, parting, knurling, drilling, boring, threading and taper turning. Give spindle speed N = 1000v/(πD), feed rate = fN, machining time = L/(fN), MRR = 1000 v f d for turning, and the rule that diameter falls by 2d per pass.

figure.title: Lathe motions
figure.aria: Block diagram of lathe parts that rotate the work and move the tool.
figure.caption: Work rotates while the carriage and cross-slide give feed and depth.

chapters.example: Turn a 50 mm diameter mild steel bar to 44 mm over 150 mm length. Cutting speed 30 m/min, feed 0.2 mm/rev, depth of cut 2 mm per pass. Find spindle speed, feed rate, machining time per pass, material removal rate, and number of passes. Check: N ≈ 191 rpm, feed rate ≈ 38.2 mm/min, time ≈ 3.93 min, MRR ≈ 12 000 mm³/min, passes = 2.
chapters.trap: Depth of cut removes twice its value from diameter; feed is mm/rev, not mm/min.
chapters.leave: CNC turning to Unit 6; gear cutting to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Drilling makes holes with a rotating multi-point tool, while milling uses a rotating cutter and a moving table; up and down milling differ in chip thickness and force direction.
chapters.depth: Drilling: twist drill geometry, point angle 118°, helix, drilling, reaming, boring, counterboring, countersinking and tapping. Give N = 1000v/(πD), feed rate fN, time = (L + approach)/(fN), MRR = (π/4)D² fN. Milling: horizontal and vertical, up milling and down milling, cutter types slab, face, end, slot and form. Simple indexing on a dividing head: crank turns = 40/N. Mention surface machining and that CNC milling is in Unit 6.

figure.title: Up and down milling
figure.aria: Block diagram comparing up milling and down milling chip thickness and feed direction.
figure.caption: In up milling the chip grows from thin to thick; down milling reverses it.

chapters.example: Drill a 20 mm diameter through hole in a 40 mm thick plate. Cutting speed 25 m/min, feed 0.15 mm/rev. Use an approach allowance of 5 mm. Find spindle speed, feed rate, drilling time and material removal rate. Check: N ≈ 398 rpm, feed rate ≈ 59.7 mm/min, time ≈ 0.754 min, MRR ≈ 18 750 mm³/min.
chapters.trap: In down milling the cutter pulls the work, so backlash must be removed; rpm uses drill diameter, not plate thickness.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 chip formation and 5.6 lathe for rotation and feed.
chapters.leave: CNC milling to Unit 6; gear hobbing to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Gear teeth are cut either by copying the tooth space with a form cutter or by generating the involute through synchronized cutter and work motion.
chapters.depth: Gear terms: module m, pitch diameter d = mz, circular pitch p = πm, addendum m, dedendum 1.25m. Forming: a form milling cutter or broach copies the tooth space; cutter number depends on tooth count. Generation: hobbing, gear shaping and rack planning create the involute by synchronized motion. Hobbing types: conventional and climb, axial and radial feeds. Some syllabi call forming copy milling. Only a few universities teach rack planning in detail. Powder metallurgy gears are in Unit 2; mention only as an alternative.

figure.aria: Tree of gear cutting methods divided into forming and generation.
figure.caption: Forming copies a cutter profile; generation makes the involute by synchronized motion.

chapters.example: Cut a 30-tooth spur gear of module 3 mm on a milling machine using a simple dividing head with 40:1 ratio. Find pitch diameter, circular pitch, addendum, dedendum, outside diameter, and the indexing crank turns. Choose a 24-hole circle. Check: d = 90 mm, p = 9.425 mm, addendum = 3 mm, dedendum = 3.75 mm, outside diameter = 96 mm, crank turns = 1 turn + 8 holes on a 24-hole circle.
chapters.trap: Forming cutter number depends on tooth count; hobbing is generation, not forming. Module is in mm, diametral pitch is in inch.
chapters.leave: Powder metallurgy gears to Unit 2; gear grinding to 5.9.

chapters.idea: Abrasive processes remove small amounts of material with hard grains to improve accuracy and surface finish; grinding, honing, lapping and superfinishing differ in tool motion and pressure.
chapters.depth: Grinding: abrasive wheel, abrasive type, grit, grade, structure and bond; wheel marking; surface, cylindrical and centerless grinding; dressing and truing; wheel speed in m/s. Honing: rotating and reciprocating abrasive stones for internal cylinders. Lapping: abrasive slurry between a lap and the work for flat or close-fit surfaces. Superfinishing: low-pressure oscillating stone, also called microfinishing. Polishing and buffing for appearance. Compare accuracy, finish, heat and applications; only a few universities teach the stone-pressure details.

figure.aria: Stack of finishing processes ordered from rougher grinding to finer superfinishing.
figure.caption: Finishing steps move from abrasive wheel to low-pressure superfinishing.

chapters.example: A surface grinding wheel of diameter 250 mm runs at 30 m/s. Find its rotational speed. The wheel is marked A 46 K 5 V 8; state the meaning of each part. Check: N ≈ 2292 rpm; A = aluminium oxide, 46 = grit, K = grade, 5 = structure, V = vitrified bond, 8 = manufacturer's record.
chapters.trap: Grinding wheel speed is in m/s; dressing sharpens the wheel while truing restores its shape; honing is not lapping.
chapters.prereq: 5.6 lathe and 5.7 milling for machine motions.
chapters.leave: Abrasive jet, EDM and other non-traditional finishing to Unit 6.

links: lathe feeds lead to drilling and milling
